lead: A service, also called a daemon, is a program that runs in the background with no terminal attached — a web server, the SSH daemon, the print spooler. Nobody types its name at a prompt, so something must start it at boot, keep it alive and stop it in a fixed order at shutdown. On modern Linux that something is systemd, the first process (PID 1), which reads plain-text unit files. This chapter shows how to start, stop, restart, reload, enable and inspect a service with systemctl, how the older service command relates to it, and where to read a service's log.
prereq: You need: Chapter 4.1 for PIDs and signals (stop means SIGTERM), and Chapter 4.2 for sudo, because every command that changes a service needs root.

sections.h3: What a service is, and who starts it

blocks.text: A service runs for days, so an administrator does not launch it by hand at a prompt. On older SysV systems the job belonged to a directory of shell scripts, /etc/init.d/. Each script answered the words start, stop, restart and status, and the service command was a thin wrapper: sudo service nginx restart ran /etc/init.d/nginx restart. Those scripts still exist on many machines, and service still works, but on a systemd machine it simply forwards the request to systemctl.

systemd is PID 1 (see Chapter 4.1). It reads unit files: plain text that describes what to run and how. A background service lives in a file ending in .service, for example nginx.service. Unit files are declarative — they state the wanted result, and systemd works out the commands. Three directories hold them:

Purpose

blocks.text: When you name a unit you may drop the suffix: systemctl start nginx and systemctl start nginx.service are the same command.

sections.h3: Starting, stopping and checking with systemctl

blocks.text: Every verb has the shape systemctl [verb] [unit]. Verbs that change state need root, so they take sudo (see Chapter 4.2).

items: start — launch the service now. It does not come back after a reboot.
stop — send SIGTERM, wait, then SIGKILL if the process ignores it (see Chapter 4.1).
restart — stop then start. The process gets a new PID and open connections drop.

reload — ask the running process to re-read its configuration, usually with SIGHUP, without dropping connections. It works only if the unit file defines ExecReload. If the unit file has no ExecReload, systemctl reload refuses the job with an error instead of re-reading anything.

status — the loaded line (which unit file, enabled or disabled), the active line (active (running) with the main PID, or inactive (dead)), and the last few log lines. Exit code 0 when active, 3 when not.
is-active — usually prints active, inactive or failed, and can briefly print activating or deactivating while a job is in progress. Made for scripts.

enable / disable — add or remove a symbolic link in the .wants directory of the target named in the unit's [Install] section — for nginx that is /etc/systemd/system/multi-user.target.wants/ — so the service is pulled in at the next boot. Neither touches the running process.
is-enabled — prints enabled, disabled or static, and can also print masked (unit blocked from starting at all) or indirect/generated in special cases.
list-unit-files --type=service and list-units --state=running — inventory of what is installed and what is up.

blocks.text: Read the two status lines separately. loaded: loaded means systemd found and parsed the unit file. active: active (running) means the process is alive right now. A unit can be loaded and inactive, or loaded and failed, and the two lines answer different questions.

A target is a named group of units that systemd brings up together. multi-user.target is the normal text-mode boot: networking, logging, SSH. graphical.target adds the display manager and pulls in multi-user.target first. Old runlevels map roughly onto them — runlevel 3 is multi-user.target, runlevel 5 is graphical.target.

items: systemctl get-default — the target reached at boot.
sudo systemctl set-default multi-user.target — make the next boot text-only.
systemctl list-dependencies multi-user.target — everything the target pulls in.

blocks.text: A service's output and errors go to the journal, not to a terminal. journalctl -u nginx shows only nginx's entries; without -u you get every unit on the machine. Add -n 50 for the last fifty lines, -f to follow live, -b for the current boot, and --since "10 min ago" for a time window.

blocks.code:
$ systemctl status nginx
$ systemctl is-active nginx
$ systemctl is-enabled nginx
$ journalctl -u nginx -n 50 --no-pager
$ journalctl -u nginx -f

blocks.text: Writing your own unit files and fixing the exact order in which targets start services belongs to advanced administration. The verbs above cover day-to-day work.

examples.question: On a lab server nginx is installed but not running; systemctl is-active nginx prints inactive. The administrator starts nginx. Status now shows active (running) with Main PID 812, and curl -I http://localhost returns HTTP/1.1 200 OK. She edits /etc/nginx/nginx.conf and restarts nginx; curl again returns HTTP/1.1 200 OK but the main PID is now 947. She then stops nginx. Give the is-active output after each of the four stages, count how many readings were active and how many inactive, and state the PID reported after the first start.
steps: Stage 1, before anything: systemctl is-active nginx prints inactive. Active count = 0, inactive count = 1.
Stage 2, after sudo systemctl start nginx: is-active prints active. Status gives Main PID 812 and curl -I answers HTTP/1.1 200 OK, so the port is served. Active count = 1, inactive count = 1.
Stage 3, after sudo systemctl restart nginx: is-active prints active. The main PID is 947, not 812, because restart killed the old process and started a new one. Active count = 2, inactive count = 1.
Stage 4, after sudo systemctl stop nginx: systemd sent SIGTERM to PID 947 and the unit is down, so is-active prints inactive. Active count = 2, inactive count = 2.
Four readings in order: inactive, active, active, inactive. Two are active, two are inactive. The PID reported after the first start is 812; after the restart it is 947.
examples.answer: The four is-active readings are inactive, active, active, inactive — 2 active and 2 inactive — and the main PID after the first start is 812 (947 after the restart).

traps: enable is not start. enable only creates a symlink so the unit is pulled in at boot; the service stays inactive until you start it or reboot.
stop is not disable. stop kills the process now; the service still starts at the next boot unless you disable it.

restart or reload? restart drops connections and changes the PID; reload re-reads the configuration in place. If the unit has no ExecReload, systemctl reload refuses the job with an error; check status afterwards.
loaded: loaded is not running. A status block can show the unit file loaded while the active line says inactive (dead). Examiners show exactly this block.
Do not grep for the word "active". systemctl status exits 0 only when the unit is active; in scripts use is-active or test that exit code.

quiz.q: Which directory holds a unit file that an administrator writes to override the copy shipped by a package?
quiz.a: /etc/systemd/system. It has higher priority than /usr/lib/systemd/system, where packages install their units.

quiz.q: Which command tells you whether nginx will start at the next boot?
quiz.a: systemctl is-enabled nginx, which prints enabled, disabled or static. is-active answers the different question of whether it is running now.

quiz.q: Why does sudo systemctl enable nginx leave the service inactive?
quiz.a: enable only creates a symbolic link in the wants directory of a target, so the boot transaction will include the unit next time. Starting the process is a separate action, done by start or by the next boot.

quiz.q: Give one situation where reload is better than restart.
quiz.a: A web server carrying live traffic. reload asks the running process (usually by SIGHUP) to re-read nginx.conf, so open connections survive and the PID stays the same; restart kills the process, drops connections and gives a new PID.

quiz.q: nginx is running and enabled. Stop it now, keep it from starting at the next boot, and confirm both states.
quiz.a: sudo systemctl stop nginx, then sudo systemctl disable nginx. Confirm with systemctl is-active nginx (prints inactive) and systemctl is-enabled nginx (prints disabled).

quiz.q: Write one command that shows only nginx's journal entries from the current boot, last 30 lines, without a pager.
quiz.a: journalctl -u nginx -b -n 30 --no-pager. The -u flag restricts output to the unit, -b to this boot, -n 30 sets the line count and --no-pager prints straight to the screen.

quiz.q: status shows active (running) with PID 812, but curl -I http://localhost cannot connect. Name two things to check and the command for each.
quiz.a: First, whether the process is actually listening on port 80 and on which address: sudo ss -ltnp | grep :80. Second, whether a firewall drops the traffic: sudo iptables -L or sudo firewall-cmd --list-all. Read journalctl -u nginx as well. The unit can be active while the server listens on a different port or address than the one you tested (for example Listen 8080 in nginx.conf), or while a firewall drops the packet. A bind failure would make the unit failed, not active.

quiz.q: A server must boot to a text console, not a graphical login, and still run nginx. Which target do you need and which commands do you use?
quiz.a: multi-user.target. Check the current default with systemctl get-default, change it with sudo systemctl set-default multi-user.target, and make sure nginx is enabled so it sits in multi-user.target.wants and is pulled in at boot.

beyond: Not for the exam. systemd has grown far past service control: .timer units replace cron for scheduled jobs, .socket units start a service only when a connection arrives, and cgroup settings inside a unit file cap memory and CPU for the whole service. Container images usually run a single process, so a container often skips systemd and the orchestrator does the restarting (see Chapter 4.6). On a real server, read man systemd.unit and man systemd.service. Search for "systemd unit file", "systemd socket activation" and "systemd timers" when you meet one.
